title: Generic Min and Max
oneLiner: Write one generic method that returns the smallest and largest item of a list of any comparable type, numbers and words alike.
keyTakeaway: A type parameter with a constraint, where T : IComparable<T>, lets one method work for every type that can be compared, with full type checking. Inside, you can only use what the constraint promises: CompareTo. Python's version just uses < and > and states the intent with type hints.
explanation:
Write MinMax(items), which returns both the smallest and the largest item of a non-empty list, in one pass. The same code must work for a list of ints and a list of strings: each test calls it on both. [3, 9, 1, 7] gives (1, 9), and ["pear", "apple", "fig"] gives ("apple", "pear"), comparing words alphabetically. Words are lowercase letters.

In C# the signature is static (T Min, T Max) MinMax<T>(List<T> items) where T : IComparable<T>. The constraint is what allows a.CompareTo(b), which is negative when a comes before b, zero when they're equal and positive when a comes after. Start with the first item as both the minimum and the maximum and update them as you go. Try it without LINQ's Min and Max, which would need two passes anyway.

In Python, def min_max(items: list[T]) -> tuple[T, T] declares the same intent with type hints (with T from Python 3.12's def min_max[T](...) syntax or a TypeVar); the code uses < and > directly and returns a tuple. The checker unpacks your pair and reports [min, max, smallest word, largest word].

starterCode.python:
def min_max(items):
    lo = items[0]
    hi = items[0]
    # TODO: one pass, using < and >.
    return lo, hi

visualizationSteps.message: Start with the first item as both min and max.
9.CompareTo(max) is positive: 9 is the new max.
1.CompareTo(min) is negative: 1 comes first, so it's the new min.
The same method on strings: CompareTo now compares alphabetically.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
def check_min_max(numbers, words):
    lo, hi = min_max(numbers)
    word_lo, word_hi = min_max(words)
    return [lo, hi, word_lo, word_hi]

complexity.note: One pass with two comparisons per item, keeping only the current minimum and maximum. Using LINQ Min and Max, or min and max, would be two passes: still O(n).
